meta.title: Texas grid, 10 days of posts
meta.subject: the Texas electric grid — ERCOT reliability, electricity prices, demand growth from data centers and industry, winterization, generation mix
meta.subtitle: Oct 6 to Oct 15, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about the Texas grid, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Data center queue is speculative bubble
lanes.description: Texas's 474 GW large-load queue (vs ~91 GW record peak) is mostly duplicate, speculative requests, so the state paused permits and the demand hype is overstated.

lanes.label: Data centers lower bills, drive growth
lanes.description: AI and data center load is an opportunity that can lower residential rates, attract massive investment like Project Star and Terafab, and justify betting on power and compute companies.

lanes.label: Firm power: gas and nuclear
lanes.description: Meeting Texas's surging demand requires dispatchable gas, nuclear and SMRs, and the grid and generators with firm capacity (Vistra, Blue Energy) are the winners.

lanes.label: Solar and batteries keep lights on
lanes.description: Texas's solar and battery buildout is why the grid handled summer easily, showing renewables plus storage deliver reliability and cheap power.

lanes.label: Texas grid fails, blame politicians
lanes.description: Texas's grid is unreliable and prone to blackouts, mocked as a failure of Texas leadership (Cruz, Abbott) and deregulated governance, often contrasted with California.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Owen Gregorian
posts.text:
Three US nuclear plants get $4.2B upgrade to add 433 MW of generating capacity | Neetika Walter, Interesting Engineering

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has offered up to $4.2 billion in conditional financing to upgrade existing nuclear plants and add 433 megawatts of generating capacity in Pennsylvania and Ohio.

The financing would support uprates and modernization across Vistra’s Beaver Valley plant in Pennsylvania and its Davis-Besse and Perry plants in Ohio. Uprating involves modifying an existing reactor so it can safely generate more electricity without building an entirely new nuclear plant.

The projects are also expected to preserve nearly 4 gigawatts of existing nuclear capacity, which the DOE says is enough to power more than 3 million homes. The additional 433 MW would help meet growing electricity demand across PJM Interconnection, the nation’s largest power grid, which serves more than 67 million people across 13 states, including Pennsylvania, Ohio, New Jersey, Virginia and Maryland, as well as Washington, D.C, and the District of Columbia.

The DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced the conditional loan commitment on Monday. Vistra must still meet technical, legal, environmental and financial requirements before the agency signs definitive financing agreements or provides any funds.

Existing reactors gain capacity

Vistra, a Texas-based power producer that operates the second-largest competitive nuclear fleet in the U.S., plans to increase electricity production at Beaver Valley, Davis-Besse and Perry without adding new transmission corridors or building equivalent new generating facilities, according to the DOE.

The investments would also support operation of the plants for an additional 20 years beyond their existing licenses. The financing package includes an option for potential future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant in Texas.

“By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, around-the-clock energy for American families and businesses,” U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said.

Nuclear uprates can increase the output of existing reactors through equipment upgrades and other changes to plant systems. In this case, the approach allows Vistra to add hundreds of megawatts while continuing to use existing nuclear sites and infrastructure.

The proposed investment comes as U.S. electricity demand is rising and policymakers seek additional sources of round-the-clock generation.

Thousands of jobs supported

The DOE estimates the planned work will support about 3,000 project-related jobs across engineering, construction and planned reactor outage work. It is also expected to preserve thousands of permanent jobs associated with the plants.

The financing advances an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in 2025 aimed at expanding U.S. nuclear generation and strengthening the domestic nuclear industry.

“These investments will extend the life of existing reactors, increase nuclear generation, and deliver abundant, around-the-clock power to lower costs and power American prosperity for decades to come,” EDF Director Gregory A. Beard said.

The $4.2 billion figure represents the maximum amount available under the conditional commitment, rather than money already awarded to Vistra. The company will receive financing only if it meets the DOE’s conditions and the two sides complete final loan documents.

https://t.co/GwhrjdrqaM

posts.name: Marc Gravely
posts.text:
South Korea and the US just announced a $22.3 billion power plant for a Texas town of 540 people.

It will be bigger than both of Texas's nuclear plants combined.

It's called Project Star: an energy campus near Encinal in La Salle County, announced on September 30.

6.47 gigawatts of natural gas generation, built to power a 5 gigawatt data center campus next door. Excess power goes back to the ERCOT grid.

The power campus will be jointly owned by the two countries, under last year's trade deal.

Nothing is built yet. First power is expected as early as 2029, and permits and approvals still have to come through.

But the location makes sense, and it starts with what's under the ground:

In October 2008, Petrohawk announced a well in La Salle County called the STS 241 #1H. It was the discovery well that opened up the Eagle Ford Shale.

Lewis Energy, which has worked in La Salle County for decades, is supplying the land, the natural gas and the water.

The Governor has told data centers to bring their own generation to the grid. This one brings South Texas gas.

At peak construction, an estimated 8,400 people will work on it. That's more than 15 times the population of Encinal.

The Eagle Ford was opened up in La Salle County in 2008. Eighteen years later, the same county could turn South Texas gas into computing power.

-Demand is strong. Management has an ongoing dialogue with every partner they’d want as a tenant, and the bar for a “standard lease” has moved up.

posts.name: CV Research
posts.text:
$BE is worth about $85 billion. $INIO is worth $14.4 billion. This year they will book almost the same revenue.

$INIO guides to $3.8 to $3.9 billion in 2026 revenue. $BE guides to $3.9 to $4.2 billion.
INNIO shipped 3.4 gigawatts of engines last year. Bloom ended 2025 with about 1 gigawatt of annual factory capacity. INNIO is building toward 10 gigawatts a year by 2030.

An AI campus needs power on a specific date and the grid cannot promise one. In the busiest regions, connecting a large new load takes five to seven years. 

Sell-side estimates value getting power one year earlier at about $4.50 per watt. INNIO's engines sell for $0.45 to $0.70 per watt. The buyer is paying for the date, not the hardware.

The J624 is a 5 megawatt gas engine that gets trucked in on a trailer and takes load in about 15 seconds. Nothing larger takes load that fast.

The demand is already on paper.

Backlog went from $1.0 billion at the end of 2024 to $6.6 billion in June. Customers have prepaid $1.4 billion. 2026 and 2027 are sold out and reservations reach into 2030 and 2031.

We traced about 8 gigawatts of Jenbacher engines to named sites. $AMZN specified 280 J620s in a Pennsylvania permit. $ORCL and OpenAI's Frontier campus runs on Jenbachers through VoltaGrid. Liberty Energy filed the first real price in an 8-K: $493 million for 100 J624s.

Then there is the part nobody prices. Services were 48% of 2025 revenue and about 65% of segment profit. A data center engine runs about 8,000 hours a year against 2,000 to 4,000 on the legacy fleet, and the parts wear by the hour. The first wave hits major overhauls from 2029.

So why is it $19.20, 29% below the $27 IPO and 55% below the June high?

Because of who is selling. The IPO was 100% secondary. The sponsors still own 86% and only about 14% of the company trades. One quarter of tariff hit margins did the rest. 

The lockup expires November 30.
Now run the math. At $19.20 the market is pricing capacity that stops at about 5.7 gigawatts, short of the Austrian expansion already under construction, with the new Wisconsin line adding nothing.

Our base case is $27, about 40% above today. Bear is $14.40 and bull is $38.

The risks are real. The Texas permit pause. A sponsor with 646 million shares to sell. VoltaGrid at 41% of 2025 orders. All of it is in the report, along with what would change our mind.

The dates that decide it: October 19 TCEQ's report, October 29 Enerflex earnings, mid November INNIO's Q3, November 30 the lockup, and around December 10 when ERCOT finishes its review.

The grid will get there eventually. The data center cannot wait for it. INNIO sells the time in between.

posts.name: VanquishTrader
posts.text:
WHY $TE COULD BE THE NEXT AI POWER MULTIBAGGER

The reason I think T1 could become one of the more asymmetric multi bagger opportunities inside the AI buildout is that the market is still valuing it like a loss making solar manufacturer today while the real thesis is what happens once G2_Austin comes online and turns the company into a much more vertically integrated U.S. power infrastructure supplier. 

G1_Dallas is already showing that the operating model can scale, with Q2 revenue nearly doubling to roughly $250M and gross margin improving toward 20% but G2 is the step change because producing cells internally instead of buying them from outside suppliers should let T1 capture much more of the economics on every module it sells. 

Management believes the initial 2.1 GW phase can eventually support roughly $375M to $450M of annualized adjusted EBITDA and a full 5 GW buildout could push that toward $650M to $700M which is a completely different earnings profile than the company investors are looking at today.

What makes that opportunity much more interesting is that the demand side is increasingly being pulled by the same AI power problem driving the rest of my energy thesis. 

Data centers need enormous amounts of new electricity and solar will not solve that problem alone, but it can become one of the fastest generation sources to deploy when paired with storage, gas and nuclear, especially in markets like ERCOT where interconnection requests are exploding and a huge percentage of the incremental load is tied to data centers. 

T1 already has several gigawatts of contracted module demand through customers like Clearway and Treaty Oak, while its domestic content strategy becomes more valuable as utilities and developers increasingly want U.S. sourced equipment that qualifies for incentives and avoids dependence on Chinese supply chains. 

If G2 works, T1 is not simply selling another commodity solar module because it can own more of the U.S. supply chain from polysilicon and wafers through cells and finished modules, which should create a better margin structure than the current business.

The valuation is where the setup starts becoming interesting because at roughly $4 to $5 per share the market is effectively making investors pay very little for the possibility that G2 actually reaches the profitability management is targeting since consensus around $0.44 of EPS in 2028 puts the stock near roughly 10x those earnings today, which is not demanding if T1 is still growing strongly beyond 2028 and G2 proves that vertically integrated domestic solar can generate sustainable margins. 

The additional optionality around Nordic data centers and battery storage makes the story even broader because T1 could eventually participate not only in supplying generation equipment to the AI buildout but also in owning pieces of the infrastructure around it which is why I think ceiling can be much higher than what a simple solar peer multiple suggests.

The risk is that none of this value exists for shareholders unless the company can actually finance the bridge between today and that future because G2 Phase 1 is expected to cost roughly $510M while unrestricted cash was only around $79M at the end of Q2, so additional debt, equity or both will almost certainly be needed before the factory reaches scale. 

That means dilution and balance sheet risk are very real, and if G2 runs over budget, ramps slowly or fails to reach the expected margin structure then the stock can stay cheap for a good reason.

But if T1 can secure financing without overwhelming existing shareholders, keep G1 margins around or above 20%, bring G2 online in 2027 and convert strong domestic demand into real free cash flow then I think the market could eventually stop viewing T1 as a speculative solar manufacturer and start valuing it as a vertically integrated U.S. power infrastructure platform sitting directly in the path of the AI electricity buildout.

posts.name: Perspez
posts.text:
$SLNH | Dorothy 3 Takes Shape: A 300 MW AI Campus Built Around Flexibility and Available Power

Soluna recently published photos on LinkedIn from its Open House in Silverton, Texas, where the company introduced Project Dorothy 3 to the local community.

One of the presentation boards caught my attention. It shows a more detailed development plan for Dorothy 3 than what I've seen in the company's earlier public materials.

The proposed 300 MW AI campus is divided into three phases:

- Phase 1: 75 MW
- Phase 2: 75 MW
- Phase 3: 150 MW

The board also appears to contain information about expected completion, although the relevant details are obscured in the photograph.

The significance here isn't simply the 300 MW figure, which Soluna has discussed for some time. It's how the company appears to be planning its development.

An interesting shift in AI infrastructure demand

Two reports from September make this particularly relevant.

On September 18, CNBC reported that OpenAI and Anthropic were exploring smaller data center deployments of approximately 20–30 MW, alongside their existing commitments to much larger AI campuses.

A day earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported that Crusoe, the developer behind OpenAI's massive Abilene data center, was expanding into smaller, factory-built modular facilities that can be transported to locations with available electricity.

Crusoe's strategy reflects growing demand for faster capacity delivery, particularly as AI inference expands. Large training campuses remain essential, but not every computing workload requires a facility with hundreds of megawatts available from day one.

That distinction matters for Dorothy 3.

An initial 75 MW phase could allow Soluna to match construction and capital requirements more closely to contracted demand, bring capacity online in stages and expand as additional power becomes available.

This isn't confirmation that Dorothy 3 will use Crusoe-style prefabricated modules. However, its proposed phase structure is consistent with the industry's increasing emphasis on flexible capacity deployment.

Dorothy 3 already has an important foundation

Unlike developers starting with undeveloped land and no nearby generating assets, Soluna has spent much of 2026 consolidating its position around Dorothy.

The company now owns the adjacent 150 MW Briscoe Wind Farm, has consolidated ownership of Dorothy 1 and completed the purchase of 397 acres for Dorothy 3.

The Briscoe substation sits directly across from the newly acquired property, providing an important starting point for the planned behind-the-meter development.

Soluna also has approximately 98 MW of existing operating infrastructure at Dorothy 1 and 2.

In September, ERCOT conditionally classified 100 MW at the existing Dorothy campus as Base Load under Batch Zero, while a separate 50 MW interconnection request remained under study. This does not constitute approval for Dorothy 3's new phases, but it highlights the value of developing alongside an established, energized campus.

There is also an important distinction between Soluna's approach and a conventional wind-only data center.

The company's strategy involves combining renewable generation with grid access and additional power resources. Soluna has discussed evaluating onsite gas generation and clustering nearby energy assets to support larger AI campuses.

That combination could be especially valuable for a phased project where power requirements increase as new data halls are developed.

The Open House photographs reveal more than the capacity plan

Another presentation board addresses the project's expected noise and nearby residences.

The material appears to reference approximately 55 dB at the facility fence, along with a map identifying one residence about 1.5 miles northeast and three residences at least 1.8 miles west of the site.

posts.text:
$VST: This Week's Rally Was the Whole Sector, and on Sector Metrics VST Is About the Same as the Peer Average

Figures in the attached infographic come from $VST 's 10-K, 10-Q and 8-K, the Q2 releases of $VST, $NRG and $TLN, the DOE press release (Oct 5, 2026), and Oct 9 closing prices. Some $NRG metrics are as of Oct 8.

$VST's 15% gain this week says little about $VST, because $CEG, $TLN and $NRG rose by similar amounts over the same days (chart 1).

The trigger was $CEG's 20-year nuclear PPA with $GOOGL on October 6. One hyperscaler contract for nuclear power was enough to re-price every independent power producer, and $VST moved within that range. The DOE's conditional loan commitment on October 5 (up to $4.2B) was $VST-specific news, but the move was no different from peers', so it is hard to call it the main driver of the week. The rate and tenor are undisclosed, conditions remain before a final agreement, and the 433MW it supports delivers between 2031 and 2034 (chart 8).

The remaining question is whether $VST deserves a different multiple than its peers now that the sector has re-rated. On guidance-based forward EV/EBITDA, $VST is at 10.7x against a 10.65x peer average. Applying the peer-average multiple to VST's earnings gives roughly today's price (chart 2). P/E is below $CEG and above $NRG and $TLN, and trailing FCF yield is the highest in the group, though $VST's separately guided pre-growth FCF is defined differently and cannot be compared directly (chart 3).

The argument for a different multiple is credit and earnings visibility. Leverage is lower than $NRG's and $TLN's (chart 4), next year's generation is mostly hedged with coverage dropping in 2028, and about half of the nuclear fleet is under long-term contract with $META and solana:5aQcoaSyy7fnhvpRHasBUAMH2nL5tTjVrmFw6BeGmoon (chart 5). Part of that is already in guidance and in the price.

PJM is the counterweight. East, which includes PJM, is the largest segment at 44% of EBITDA, so price caps or market-rule discussions can hit $VST harder than the sector average (chart 6). EV per kW sits below new-build cost and well above the Cogentrix purchase price, so it reads as cheap or expensive depending on the benchmark and is a reference only (chart 7).

Many accounts credit the Pelosi household's trades for the attention on this stock. Disclosures show 50 call options in the spouse's name exercised in January 2026 into 5,000 shares. The buying decision dates from early 2025, so it was not used in this analysis.

Four points for investors to watch.

This week's move was a sector factor. $VST-specific and sector variables need to be separated.
Forward EV/EBITDA is almost the same as the peer average. Whether a premium or discount is justified depends on how 2027 guidance (expected early next year) and Q3 results (expected early November, date unconfirmed) include Cogentrix and $META.
Low leverage, a BBB− rating and high hedge ratios are strengths. The 2028 hedge ratio, the Cogentrix closing and uprate capex through 2034 are variables.
East carries the largest weight, so PJM price caps, market rules and the 2027 ERCOT forward curve can move the stock ahead of the sector metrics.

posts.text:
写完核电龙头 Constellation之后，我们今天来看一下一直在list上但却没有聊过的 Vistra。

它和 CEG 是天生一对镜像：CEG 是"核电卖 AI 最领先、估值也最贵"的那个；Vistra 则是"比 CEG 落后一步、但也便宜一截"的那个。 过去两年，整个电力板块都被 AI 数据中心"缺电"的叙事抬上了天，Vistra 2024 年是标普 500 全年涨幅第二名仅次于 Palantir，涨了 261%甚至还把英伟达都甩在后面。

先简单说下它是谁：全美最大的独立发电商（IPP）之一 + 零售一体化，大本营在德州 ERCOT，总装机约 43.6 吉瓦，还有约 500 万零售客户，旗舰品牌 TXU Energy。这里有个特别关键、也特别容易被忽略的点：市场谈它的 AI 核电故事谈得很热，但它的核电只占装机的 15%，真正扛起大半收入的是那 62% 的天然气，外加 20% 的煤。 换句话说它不是一支干干净净的"核电纯多"，而是一个"又脏又全"的综合发电商。

它的身世也挺传奇：前身是德州电力巨头 TXU，2007 年被 KKR、TPG、高盛用约 450 亿美元做了史上最大的杠杆收购，这里连巴菲特都掺了一脚、后来认错，结果页岩气来了、煤电算盘落空，2014 年破产，这应该是美国史上最大的非金融破产之一。Vistra 就是从这片废墟里重组、重生出来的，然后一路靠并购做大，2024 年收 Energy Harbor 拿到了四台核电。

看它的财报别看 GAAP 净利润，要看"调整后 EBITDA"因为它用大量电价对冲，账面浮盈浮亏把净利润打得上蹿下跳，你去看2021/22 还亏二十多亿，2年之后2024 居然赚二十八亿。但如果你去看 EBITDA 就正常了，五年从约 20 亿涨到约 59 亿，稳稳向上，还刚升了投资级、疯狂回购把股本缩了 30%。

那 AI 这波它吃到了多少？ 

坦白说 2024 年它是落后 CEG 和 Talen 的。但 2026 年它一口气补了四张大牌：Meta（PJM 核电、逾 2,600 兆瓦、20 年）、AWS（德州 Comanche Peak、至多 1,200 兆瓦、20 年）、英伟达/KKR 的 Helix 合资、以及 DOE 至多 42 亿美元的有条件贷款。所以它从"落后但便宜"，正在变成"追上了、但还便宜"。

但便宜也是有原因的：

一是它不干净：核电只 15%、八成是又脏又周期的气和煤，商品价格敞口大、没有受监管公用事业那种"保证回报率"的保护伞；而且 CEO 自己都承认，德州电价最近在走软。

二是 Moss Landing 那把火：2025 年初它在加州的储能项目起火，冲销了约 4 亿、还惹上一堆官司和清理。

三是它脆：2025 年初 DeepSeek 一来，它单日暴跌约 28%，是所有 AI 电力股里跌得最惨的，同天 CEG 跌 21%、英伟达跌 17%。

以前大家说"VST 杠杆是 CEG 的好几倍"，但这个已经过时了。CEG 收了 Calpine 之后自己也背上巨债，净债涨到约 240 亿，绝对值反而超过了 Vistra 的约 195 亿。现在两家杠杆率半斤八两，VST 甚至还略低。所以 Vistra 便宜不是因为它杠杆更高，而是因为它那套"又脏又周期"的组合天生就该比纯核电的 CEG 有着更低的估值。

我认为Vistra 是一个"确实便宜、叙事也在追上，但绝不是'干净'故事"的标的。它前瞻 PE 约 16 倍，CEG 要 22 倍以上、自由现金流收益率约 7.2%，而这部分CEG 才 3.8%，便宜了一大截；但你买的不是纯核电，而是一个带着三倍 EBITDA 的债、八成化石燃料、外加一桩火灾官司的综合发电商。它更适合"看好 AI 缺电、但嫌 CEG 太贵、愿意为便宜承担更多杠杆和周期波动"的人，而不是想买一份"干净确定性"的人。

拐点则需要关注那些数据中心大单的 EBITDA 能不能从 2027 年起稳稳爬坡、ERCOT 电价能不能止跌、Moss Landing 官司最终花多少、去杠杆守不守得住。

下一个验证点是 Q3 2026 财报，大约 11 月初。

立场：中立 · 无持仓 · DYODR。

posts.text:
Texas just hit PAUSE on data centers.

474 gigawatts are waiting in line for power. The most Texas has ever used at once: 91. LOL.

✅ BofA: Texas has a 474 GW line of requests to plug into the grid. About 90% is data centers.
✅ That's more than 5 times the grid's all-time record.
✅ The state paused its big grid study, stopped approving hookups of 75 MW or more, and ordered a halt to all data center permits.
✅ Not just Texas. Pause or moratorium proposals show up in 20 of this year's 36 governor races.
➡️ Sounds like a disaster for AI, right? Nope.
➡️ When it gets harder to build, whoever ALREADY has capacity gets to charge a premium. Think Microsoft, SpaceX, Meta, Amazon, Google.
➡️ Who gets hosed: the smaller neoclouds that still need financing to build.
✅ BofA's read: the money sorts, it doesn't stop.
😇 Zero chance of a federal pause.
🚨 The risk: this isn't settled on election night. The Texas grid audit lands Dec 10 and the final answer is a 2027 story. If real projects get cut, the build slows.
➡️ Bottom line: the pause squeezes the little guys and hands the giants pricing power.

$VST remains one of my favorite ways to play rising U.S. power demand.

Vistra is already benefiting from stronger pricing. Q2 adjusted EBITDA increased more than 30% YoY to $1.77B, driven primarily by higher realized energy and capacity prices along with contributions from acquired assets. Management continues to expect major load growth through 2030, which is roughly 4-6% annually in ERCOT and 2-3% in PJM driven by data centers, reshoring, electrification and population growth.

The nuclear story is even more compelling. Vistra signed 20-year agreements with Meta covering 2,609 MW across its PJM nuclear fleet, including 433 MW of new uprates. It also has a 20-year agreement with AWS for up to 1,200 MW from Comanche Peak.

The DOE has announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2B to help finance nuclear uprates and modernization across Vistra's Pennsylvania and Ohio fleet. If finalized, that financing would help preserve nearly 4 GW of existing nuclear generation while adding 433 MW of new capacity.

And the financial setup remains strong. Vistra's 2027 adjusted EBITDA midpoint opportunity is $7.4B-$7.8B and importantly, that figure excludes potential contributions from the pending Cogentrix acquisition AND the Meta PPAs. Vistra has also repurchased roughly $6.5B of stock since 2021, reducing its share count by ~30%.

Management summed up the opportunity well on the latest earnings call: “the long-term expected improvement in power market fundamentals is underway.”

TLDR; Higher realized power prices. Rapid electricity demand growth. 20-year nuclear contracts. Potentially billions in federal financing. Aggressive buybacks.

I really like the long-term setup for $VST.

posts.text:
$IREN: The ERCOT Advantage

I do not take any paid sponsorships/promotions but I get alot of free trials from various platforms. If I spot something useful in the data, I'll make a post explaining what I see; similar to quoting a good post.

ERCOT vs PJM
From @OrnnExchange run by @wayne_nelmz, one of the charts is price of power. In a recent $NBIS interview, a former product manager admitted that electricity was the third biggest cost after GPUs and financing (1). $48/MWh in ERCOT or $124/MWh in PJM doesn't seem like alot but when you run power hungry over 5 years, its a very significant operations cost. For 1,000 MW × 8,760 hours/year × 5 years × $124/MWh = $5.431 billion. A 1GW buildout cost ~$50B so electricity is 10% the cost it takes to initial build out. 

Economics
Thus for a 300MW site like Vineland, running in ERCOT instead of PJM would be (124-48)=$76/MWh cheaper or 300 MW × 8,760 hours/year × 5 years x $76/MWh = 1B cheaper. 

The economics of a 1.1 PUE site in PJM would be effectively 2.83 PUE since electricity cost 2.58x more. 

Volatility
Besides economics, volatility matters. Furthermore, PJM is coming from a 40% MoM increase while ERCOT is coming on a 21.59% increase. Part of this volatility is just hot summer pricing but some of it is long term trend.
